executive_summary.title: Executive Summary
executive_summary.content: Neutral atom quantum processors employ optical tweezer arrays to manipulate rubidium and cesium atoms [cite_exec_c1]. Recent experiments achieve two-qubit Rydberg controlled-Z gate fidelities of 99.5% [cite_exec_c2], and surface code simulations demonstrate favorable fault-tolerance thresholds [cite_exec_c3].

sections.title: Processor Architectures and Gate Fidelities
sections.content: Neutral atom quantum computing platforms rely on two-dimensional optical tweezer arrays to position rubidium-87 and cesium-133 atoms with sub-micron precision [cite_cite_3]. Experimental setups have attained two-qubit Rydberg controlled-Z gate fidelities reaching 99.5% through adiabatic passage pulses [cite_cite_4]. Additionally, dual-species configurations facilitate non-destructive mid-circuit syndrome measurements that avoid decohering neighboring data qubits [cite_cite_5].

sections.title: Fault-Tolerance Thresholds and Surface Codes
sections.content: Simulations of surface codes on hexagonal and square neutral atom grids reveal a fault-tolerance threshold of 1.25% when accounting for realistic atom loss and photon scattering noise models [cite_cite_6]. To accomplish a logical error rate below 1e-6 per gate, a distance-7 rotated surface code needs 98 physical data qubits and 97 auxiliary syndrome qubits for every logical qubit block [cite_cite_7].

Recent experiments achieve two-qubit Rydberg controlled-Z gate fidelities of 99.5% [cite_exec_c2], and surface code simulations demonstrate favorable fault-tolerance thresholds [cite_exec_c3].

claims.text: Neutral atom quantum computers utilize two-dimensional optical tweezer arrays to dynamically rearrange individual rubidium-87 and cesium-133 atoms with sub-micron positional precision.
Recent experiments achieved two-qubit Rydberg controlled-Z gate fidelities of 99.5% using adiabatic passage pulses.

sections.title: Processor Architectures and Gate Fidelities
sections.content: Neutral atom quantum computing platforms rely on two-dimensional optical tweezer arrays to position rubidium-87 and cesium-133 atoms with sub-micron precision [cite_cite_3]. Experimental setups have attained two-qubit Rydberg controlled-Z gate fidelities reaching 99.5% through adiabatic passage pulses [cite_cite_4]. Additionally, dual-species configurations facilitate non-destructive mid-circuit syndrome measurements that avoid decohering neighboring data qubits [cite_cite_5].

sections.title: Fault-Tolerance Thresholds and Surface Codes
sections.content: Simulations of surface codes on hexagonal and square neutral atom grids reveal a fault-tolerance threshold of 1.25% when accounting for realistic atom loss and photon scattering noise models [cite_cite_6]. To accomplish a logical error rate below 1e-6 per gate, a distance-7 rotated surface code needs 98 physical data qubits and 97 auxiliary syndrome qubits for every logical qubit block [cite_cite_7].

conclusion.title: Conclusion
conclusion.content: Neutral atom arrays provide high-fidelity control capabilities and defined fault-tolerance thresholds [cite_cite_8]. The demonstrated two-qubit gate fidelities and surface code threshold simulations support the continued development of this quantum architecture [cite_cite_9].

claims.text: Neutral atom arrays utilize two-dimensional optical tweezer arrays and achieve high fidelity control as demonstrated in recent experiments.
Surface code simulations on neutral atom grids demonstrate a fault-tolerance threshold of 1.25% under realistic noise models.

limitations: Limited availability of long-term multi-qubit physical scaling data beyond small logical blocks.
Dependence on specific noise models such as atom loss and photon scattering rates which may vary in hardware implementations.
